sets.title: Law and method changes
sets.what: Changes since 2016 that break year-to-year comparisons.
rows: Laws 2013 c 131: no-excuse absentee voting (first general 2014); 46-day absentee period (s.203B.081 subd 1)
Laws 2016 c 161: in the last 7 days voters could feed absentee ballots directly into a tabulator ('direct balloting') [I effect from history line]
2016-2022 in-person absentee mostly cast in the last week as direct balloting.
2020 consent decree waived the absentee witness and allowed ballots postmarked by ED received within 7 days; Carson v. Simon (8th Cir., 10/29/2020) ordered late ballots segregated
2020 mail behaviour and receipt differ from 2018/2022/2024/2026.

Laws 2023 c 62 art 4: 18-day early voting (s.203B.081 subd 1a) for elections on/after 1/1/2024; Laws 2023 c 34: automatic voter registration (s.201.161), pre-registration, permanent absentee voter status (s.203B.04 subd 5)
2024 and 2026 have 18-day early voting and a permanent absentee list; 2016-2022 did not. AVR inflates the registration denominator from 2023: per-registrant rates fall mechanically.
Laws 2025 c 39 art 8 amended s.201.161 (automatic registration must exclude people without documentary proof of citizenship) and s.203B.081
Registration flows after 2025 differ from 2023-24 AVR flows.

Ballot boards may open accepted envelopes and deposit ballots after close of business on the 19th day before ED (s.203B.121 subd 4); counted on ED; mail ballots received after 8 p.m. ED are late (s.203B.08)
Absentee results post early on election night.

sets.title: Litigation
rows: Minnesota City of Oak Grove Electronic Roster Challenge
City of Oak Grove v. Simon et al
An anti-voting lawsuit challenging a Minnesota law requiring electronic rosters over paper rosters at polling sites.
The Minnesota Supreme Court granted the City of Oak Grove’s petition, allowing the city election officials to decide whether or not to only use paper rosters for the midterm election.
R (Democracy Docket case page opened 2026-10-25; Democratic-aligned tracker, framing is theirs; court filings linked on the page not opened)
Public Interest Legal Foundation v. Simon
Lawsuit filed by the Public Interest Legal Foundation challenging the state’s exemption from the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA).
R (Democracy Docket case page opened 2026-10-25; Democratic-aligned tracker, framing is theirs; court filings linked on the page not opened)
Minnesota DOJ Voter Data Access Challenge
An anti-voting lawsuit seeking to compel Minnesota to provide the DOJ with access to its statewide voter registration data.

The 8th Circuit granted the DOJ’s motion to expedite the appeal to the extent it seeks expedited briefing but denied to the extent it seeks an expedited decision after submission of the case to the court.
R (Democracy Docket case page opened 2026-10-25; Democratic-aligned tracker, framing is theirs; court filings linked on the page not opened)
Minnesota Voters Alliance v. City of Minneapolis
An anti-voting lawsuit seeking to require Minneapolis to staff early-voting sites with bipartisan election judges ahead of the 2026 election.

The Minnesota Supreme Court ruled in favor of MVA, ordering election judges to be present at polling locations for early voting to “resolve challenges to a voter’s status and to administer the vouching process for voter registration.”
R (Democracy Docket case page opened 2026-10-25; Democratic-aligned tracker, framing is theirs; court filings linked on the page not opened)
Minnesota Alliance for Retired Americans v. Simon

Lawsuit filed by the Minnesota Alliance for Retired Americans and two voters against Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon (D) challenging the state’s requirement that absentee voters obtain the signature of a witness to cast an absentee ballot.
R (Democracy Docket case page opened 2026-10-25; Democratic-aligned tracker, framing is theirs; court filings linked on the page not opened)

rows: Minnesota Alter Management and Investment Policies for Permanent School Fund Amendment

Amend the constitution to change the administrative policies surrounding the investment and distribution of the Minnesota Permanent School Fund, specifically to state that the management of the fund would need to preserve the purchasing power of the fund over time.[97]
